question: How do you configure form login in Spring Security?
title: Configuring Form Login in Spring Security — SecurityFilterChain
direct_answer: Configure form login with formLogin() in a SecurityFilterChain. If form login is enabled and no custom page is supplied, Spring Security can generate a login page at /login. A custom configuration can set the page, processing URL, parameter names, and success or failure handlers. A JSON API may use handlers with a session-based login or choose a separate bearer-token flow; REST does not force one authentication style.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of configuring form login for both traditional web apps and REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Protecting a custom login page so it redirects to itself, disabling CSRF while still using cookie authentication, or assuming every JSON API needs JWT
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate the credential-processing URL from the page, explain session persistence and CSRF, and choose redirects or JSON handlers from the client flow

sections.title: Configuring Form Login for Different Application Types
sections.content:
Spring Security provides **formLogin()** for username/password authentication in a SecurityFilterChain. When it is enabled without a custom page, Spring Security can generate a page at /login. A custom setup can name the HTML page, the URL that processes the submitted credentials, the field names, and the success and failure handlers.

Server-rendered browser applications commonly redirect after login and save the SecurityContext in an HTTP session. A JavaScript client can instead use success and failure handlers that write JSON while still using a session cookie. A separate bearer-token flow is another design, but it is not required merely because endpoints return JSON. If a browser authenticates with cookies, keep CSRF protection in the design.

sections.title: formLogin() Knobs
sections.content:
blue|Generated page|~quick start|formLogin(withDefaults()) can provide /login|username and password fields|CSRF is part of the browser flow
emerald|Custom browser page|~redirect flow|loginPage() serves the HTML|loginProcessingUrl() receives credentials|permit the page and related URLs
amber|JSON client|~choose the credential model|handlers can write JSON with a session|bearer tokens are another option|CSRF follows automatically sent credentials

sections.title: Form Login Configuration for REST API with JSON Responses
When to Use Each Configuration Style
sections.content:
Use the generated login page for learning and quick internal prototypes. Use a custom page and redirect handlers for server-rendered browser applications. A browser client that expects JSON can use custom success and failure handlers and still keep authentication in a session.

For an API whose client explicitly sends bearer access tokens, configure OAuth 2.0 Resource Server rather than assuming a handwritten JWT filter is required. Form login and stateless bearer authentication are different flows; select one from the client, credential storage, logout, CSRF, and revocation requirements.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Protecting the custom login page**: if every request requires authentication and /login is not permitted, the browser can enter a redirect loop.
- **Mismatching page and processing URLs**: the form action must post to the configured loginProcessingUrl and use the configured parameter names.
- **Returning redirects to a JSON-only client**: choose handlers whose response contract matches the client.
- **Combining STATELESS with an expected browser login session**: credential processing may succeed, but the SecurityContext will not be saved in an HTTP session for later requests.
- **Disabling CSRF because the response is JSON**: cookie-based authentication can still be exposed to CSRF.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **formLogin() DSL**: Fluent API in SecurityFilterChain that configures UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter and related components
**Default login page**: Spring Boot auto-generates /login with username/password fields when you call formLogin() without loginPage()
**loginProcessingUrl()**: The URL where the login form posts credentials (default matches loginPage, e.g., POST /login)
**Custom handlers**: AuthenticationSuccessHandler and AuthenticationFailureHandler can return JSON instead of redirecting when that matches the client contract
**Parameter names**: usernameParameter() and passwordParameter() let you rename the form field names if your frontend uses email/pass instead of username/password

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Configure form login with formLogin in a SecurityFilterChain. When no custom page is supplied, Spring Security can generate /login. A custom setup can name the page, credential-processing URL, username and password fields, and success or failure handlers. Server-rendered applications commonly redirect and save the SecurityContext in an HTTP session. A JSON client can use handlers that write JSON and still use a session, or it can use a separate bearer-token design. The choice is not determined by the word REST. If authentication is held in a cookie, include CSRF protection. If the session policy is STATELESS, do not expect a successful form login to persist authentication into later requests.

question: What happens on login failure in Spring Security?
title: Spring Security Login Failure — Authentication Exceptions
direct_answer: A failed form-login attempt is passed to an AuthenticationFailureHandler with an AuthenticationException. DaoAuthenticationProvider normally hides UsernameNotFoundException as BadCredentialsException, which helps avoid revealing whether a username exists. A browser flow commonly redirects to /login?error; a JSON flow can return a generic 401 response. Public messages and timing should not expose account existence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of authentication failure handling and security implications of different error messages
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing whether a username exists by returning different error messages for missing user vs wrong password
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the user enumeration security risk and why Spring hides the distinction between wrong username and wrong password by default

sections.title: Authentication Failure Exception Hierarchy and Security
sections.content:
When authentication fails, Spring Security reports an **AuthenticationException** to the configured AuthenticationFailureHandler. Examples include BadCredentialsException, LockedException, DisabledException, AccountExpiredException, and CredentialsExpiredException.

DaoAuthenticationProvider hides UsernameNotFoundException as BadCredentialsException by default. Keep the public result generic because different messages for a missing username and a wrong password can reveal valid accounts. Internally, log or publish an authentication event with enough context for monitoring, but never include the submitted password. The handler decides the HTTP behavior: a form-login browser flow commonly redirects to /login?error, while an API-style handler may write a generic 401 response. Spring does not prescribe a universal 403 mapping for locked or disabled accounts.

sections.title: Failure Exceptions at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|BadCredentialsException|~credential failure|often also hides missing user|return a generic public message|do not reveal account existence
amber|LockedException / DisabledException|~account state|may arise from UserDetails flags|public response is application policy|avoid enumeration leaks
blue|AuthenticationFailureHandler|~chooses the response|redirect for a browser flow|JSON status for an API flow|publish safe audit events separately

sections.title: Custom Failure Handler with Security-Conscious Error Messages
When to Customize Failure Handling
sections.content:
Use a custom failure handler when the client needs JSON instead of a redirect or when the application must publish a safe audit event. A generic 401 response is a common API contract; a separate support or recovery flow can explain how a user should proceed without revealing account state at login.

Brute-force protection and account lockout need an application-wide design that handles concurrency, distributed instances, trusted client addresses, recovery, and denial-of-service risk. They should not be reduced to a blocking database update or delay inside one failure handler. A simple browser application can keep the configured redirect to /login?error.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Exposing user enumeration**: keep missing-user and wrong-password responses indistinguishable, and consider account-state messages carefully.
- **Logging sensitive data**: never log submitted passwords or bearer credentials.
- **Assuming exception-to-status mappings**: configure and test the application's own browser redirect or JSON status contract.
- **Naive lockout updates**: a safe design must handle races, multiple application instances, recovery, and attacks that deliberately lock other users out.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **AuthenticationException hierarchy**: Base exception with subclasses like BadCredentialsException, LockedException, DisabledException for specific failure reasons
**User enumeration protection**: DaoAuthenticationProvider converts UsernameNotFoundException to BadCredentialsException so missing user and wrong password look identical
**AuthenticationFailureHandler**: Interface with single method onAuthenticationFailure that processes exceptions and determines the response
**Form-login response**: the configured failure handler commonly redirects to /login?error; it does not need to expose the exception text
**API response**: a generic 401 is a common choice, while account-state status and recovery behavior are application policy

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: When form authentication fails, Spring Security passes an AuthenticationException to the configured AuthenticationFailureHandler. DaoAuthenticationProvider hides UsernameNotFoundException as BadCredentialsException by default so a missing user and a wrong password need not look different to the client. Other internal exceptions can describe locked, disabled, or expired accounts, but the public status and message are application policy and should not reveal valid usernames. A browser flow commonly redirects to /login?error; a JSON flow can return a generic 401 body. Record safe audit information separately and never log the submitted password.

question: What is the Spring Security logout flow?
title: Spring Security Logout Flow — Session Invalidation and Cleanup
direct_answer: With the usual form-login configuration, a POST to /logout is handled by LogoutFilter before authorization. Configured LogoutHandlers perform actions such as invalidating the HTTP session, clearing authentication and the SecurityContextRepository, and optionally deleting selected cookies. A LogoutSuccessHandler then redirects or writes a response. With CSRF enabled, the logout request needs a valid CSRF token.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of secure logout implementation and session cleanup mechanisms in Spring Security
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming client-side cookie or token deletion always revokes the server-side credential, or assuming Spring deletes every cookie automatically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the configured LogoutHandlers, CSRF-aware request matching, session invalidation, cookie cleanup, and the separate revocation policy for bearer access and refresh tokens

sections.title: Understanding Spring Security Logout Flow
sections.content:
Spring Security's servlet logout support matches a logout request in LogoutFilter, runs the configured LogoutHandlers, and then invokes a LogoutSuccessHandler. In a common session-based configuration, SecurityContextLogoutHandler clears authentication and the SecurityContext and invalidates the HTTP session. A configured SecurityContextRepository is also cleared. CookieClearingLogoutHandler, remember-me support, or a Clear-Site-Data header can remove selected client state when configured.

With CSRF enabled, the default logout request uses POST and needs a valid CSRF token. Do not treat GET logout as a harmless read. Bearer-token logout is a separate lifecycle problem: removing a token from one client does not revoke another copy. The design may combine bounded access-token lifetime with refresh-token revocation or rotation, a denylist, introspection, or another issuer-supported control.

sections.title: Logout Flow Step by Step
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Matching logout request
POST + CSRF token by default] --> B[LogoutFilter] B --> C[Run configured LogoutHandlers] C --> D[Clear authentication and SecurityContext] C --> E[Invalidate HTTP session when configured] C --> F[Clear selected cookies or tokens when configured] D --> G[LogoutSuccessHandler] E --> G F --> G G --> H[Configured redirect or response] ```

sections.title: Configuring Logout in Spring Security
When to Customize Logout Behavior
sections.content:
Use the standard session logout handlers for a browser application when their cleanup matches the application's state. Customize the LogoutSuccessHandler only for the final redirect or response. Put cleanup in a LogoutHandler or a separate token-revocation workflow, for example clearing application session data or revoking a refresh token.

External calls and audit delivery need deliberate failure behavior; do not make successful local logout depend blindly on an unavailable remote service. Configure cookie deletion only for cookies the application owns, and test the result in the deployed container and proxy setup.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming every cookie is deleted**: session invalidation and explicit cookie deletion are different actions; configure and test the cookies the application owns.
- **Using GET for a state-changing logout**: with CSRF protection enabled, use the default POST flow and send the CSRF token.
- **Treating client deletion as revocation**: a copied bearer access token can remain usable until the issuer or resource server rejects it.
- **Copying one JWT recipe**: access-token lifetime, refresh rotation, denylists, and introspection have different security and operating costs.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **LogoutFilter**: intercepts POST requests to /logout and coordinates the entire logout process by calling registered handlers
**LogoutHandler**: interface for custom cleanup logic like session invalidation, cookie deletion, or external API calls during logout
**LogoutSuccessHandler**: handles post-logout behavior such as redirecting to a login page or returning JSON for REST APIs
**CSRF protection**: logout requires POST by default to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks that force users to log out
**Session invalidation**: calling invalidateHttpSession(true) destroys the HttpSession and removes it from server memory

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In the usual form-login setup, POST /logout is handled by LogoutFilter before request authorization. It runs the configured LogoutHandlers and then a LogoutSuccessHandler. SecurityContextLogoutHandler can clear authentication and the SecurityContext and invalidate the HTTP session. Selected cookies are removed only when remember-me support or a cookie-clearing handler is configured; session invalidation does not mean every browser cookie is deleted. With CSRF enabled, the POST includes a valid CSRF token. For a bearer-token system, deleting a token from one client does not revoke a stolen copy. The application needs an explicit access- and refresh-token lifecycle, which may use bounded lifetimes, refresh-token rotation or revocation, introspection, or a denylist according to the risk.

question: What is the difference between form login and HTTP Basic authentication in Spring?
title: Form Login vs HTTP Basic Auth in Spring Security
direct_answer: Form login collects credentials with an HTML form and commonly keeps the resulting SecurityContext in a session. HTTP Basic sends a Base64-encoded username and password in the Authorization header on each authenticated request and challenges with 401 plus WWW-Authenticate. Basic itself has no login form, but whether Spring also uses a session depends on session and context-repository configuration. Both require HTTPS because Base64 is not encryption.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of different authentication mechanisms and when to use each based on client type and security requirements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling HTTP Basic inherently stateless, claiming JWT is automatically safer, or using either credential flow without TLS
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate the wire protocol from Spring's session policy and compare browser behavior, credential replay, logout, and client needs without declaring a universal winner

sections.title: Comparing Form Login and HTTP Basic Authentication
sections.content:
**Form login** is a browser-oriented username/password flow. An unauthenticated browser is commonly redirected to an HTML page, credentials are submitted to the processing URL, and the resulting SecurityContext is usually saved in an HTTP session. Later requests carry the session cookie rather than the password.

**HTTP Basic** is an HTTP challenge-response scheme. The client sends Base64-encoded username and password in the Authorization header on each request for which it uses the credential. The server challenges with 401 and WWW-Authenticate. Basic has no login page of its own. It is often configured with a stateless session policy, but the protocol does not prevent Spring from saving the resulting SecurityContext when a session repository and policy allow it. Both must use TLS because Base64 provides no confidentiality.

sections.title: Picking an Auth Style
sections.content:
blue|Form Login|~browser-oriented|commonly saves context in a session|redirects to an HTML login page|later requests use a cookie
emerald|HTTP Basic|~HTTP challenge scheme|credentials sent in Authorization|401 + WWW-Authenticate challenge|session behavior is separately configured
amber|Bearer token|~another API option|client sends an access token|needs expiry and revocation policy|not automatically safer than every alternative

rows: Usually configured stateless; Spring session policy is separate
Browser shows popup dialog or 401 response
Server tracks session with JSESSIONID cookie
Depends on session policy; Basic itself has no login cookie

sections.title: Form Login Configuration (Browsers)
HTTP Basic Configuration (APIs/Tools)
When to Use Each Authentication Method
sections.content:
Use **form login** when a browser application needs an HTML sign-in experience and a server-managed login session. JSON handlers can adapt the response for a JavaScript client when sessions still fit the design.

Use **HTTP Basic** for simple clients that can safely hold and resend a credential, often for controlled tools or narrow integrations. Configure a stateless policy explicitly if that is required, and use TLS. For delegated authorization or broader machine-to-machine systems, standards such as OAuth 2.0 client credentials, mTLS, or a managed identity may fit better. A bearer JWT avoids resending the password but introduces token issuance, validation, exposure, expiry, and revocation concerns; it is not automatically the most secure REST choice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using HTTP Basic without TLS**: Base64 is reversible encoding, so transport security is required.
- **Calling Basic inherently stateless**: set and test the session-creation and SecurityContextRepository behavior instead of inferring it from the Authorization header.
- **Returning an HTML redirect to a JSON-only client**: configure an entry point or authentication flow that matches the client.
- **Calling JWT automatically safer**: bearer tokens can also be stolen and replayed; compare credential exposure, lifetime, revocation, and client storage.
- **Parsing credentials by hand**: use maintained Spring Security support unless the protocol truly requires custom behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **State policy**: form login commonly persists authentication in a session; HTTP Basic is commonly configured stateless, but Spring's policy decides
**UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter**: processes form login by intercepting POST requests to /login and validating credentials
**BasicAuthenticationFilter**: extracts Base64-encoded credentials from Authorization header and authenticates each request independently
**WWW-Authenticate header**: HTTP Basic sends this header in 401 responses telling clients to provide credentials in specified format
**HTTPS requirement**: both methods send credentials over network and require TLS encryption to prevent interception and credential theft

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Form login collects username and password through an HTML form and commonly saves the successful SecurityContext in an HTTP session. The browser then sends a session cookie, not the password, on later requests. HTTP Basic has no login page: the client sends a Base64-encoded username and password in the Authorization header, and the server challenges missing credentials with 401 and WWW-Authenticate. Basic is commonly paired with a stateless session policy, but that is a Spring configuration choice rather than a property that forbids sessions. Both flows require TLS. For example, a server-rendered employee portal can use form login and a session cookie, while a controlled command-line client can send an HTTP Basic header on each request. A JSON API can also use sessions, opaque bearer tokens, or JWTs depending on credential storage, revocation, and operating requirements; JWT is not automatically safer.

question: What is the Spring Security form login flow?
title: Spring Security Form Login Flow — Authentication Process
direct_answer: In the default form-login flow, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter reads username and password form parameters from the configured processing URL and asks AuthenticationManager to authenticate them. A DaoAuthenticationProvider can load the user through UserDetailsService and verify the stored password through PasswordEncoder. On success, the Authentication is placed in the SecurityContext and is normally saved for later requests by the configured SecurityContextRepository, commonly an HTTP session repository.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the complete authentication chain and each component's role in form-based authentication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating authentication as a black box without knowing the sequence of filters, managers, providers, and services involved
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the two-phase nature: unauthenticated token creation by filter, then authenticated token creation by provider after verification

sections.title: Spring Security Form Login Authentication Chain
sections.content:
The default form-login pipeline has clear responsibilities. **UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter** reads username and password request parameters from the login-processing request and creates an unauthenticated token. **AuthenticationManager**, usually ProviderManager, delegates to a provider that supports that token. **DaoAuthenticationProvider** uses **UserDetailsService** to load stored user details and **PasswordEncoder** to verify the submitted password against the encoded value.

On success, the filter places the returned authenticated token in the **SecurityContext**, invokes the success handler, and saves the context through the configured SecurityContextRepository. A common browser setup uses an HTTP session repository so later requests can restore authentication. The exact persistence and success or failure behavior are configurable; form login itself should not be described as an unchangeable JWT opposite.

sections.title: Form Login Authentication Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Login-processing POST
username + password] --> B[UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter
builds unauthenticated token] B --> C[AuthenticationManager
commonly ProviderManager] C --> D[Supporting AuthenticationProvider] D --> E[For DaoAuthenticationProvider:
UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder] E --> G{Authentication result} G -->|success| H[Authenticated token
placed in SecurityContext] H --> J[Configured repository
may save context] G -->|failure| I[AuthenticationFailureHandler
configured response] ```

sections.title: Form Login Configuration with Custom UserDetailsService
When to Use Form Login
sections.content:
Form login fits a browser application that submits an HTML login form and benefits from success and failure navigation plus a server-managed session. The authentication provider behind it may load users from a database, LDAP, or another configured source.

An API or SPA may instead use a session with API-specific handlers, OAuth 2.0/OIDC login, or bearer access tokens. Choose from the client, identity provider, logout and revocation needs, CSRF model, and user experience rather than assuming a particular application type always requires JWT.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting a controller to handle the processing URL**: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter handles the configured login-processing request before MVC.
- **Copying an internal filter position**: rely on Spring Security's configuration and documented filter-order contracts rather than a numeric position from one version.
- **Confusing persistence with authentication**: successful form authentication creates a SecurityContext; a SecurityContextRepository decides whether and where it is saved.
- **Confusing CSRF with XSS**: CSRF protects unsafe browser requests that automatically carry authentication. It does not prevent injected script. Include the configured CSRF token in the login form when protection applies.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter**: handles the configured login-processing request and reads username/password form parameters
**AuthenticationManager**: Facade interface (usually ProviderManager) that delegates to one or more AuthenticationProvider implementations
**DaoAuthenticationProvider**: Default provider that uses UserDetailsService to load user and PasswordEncoder to verify password hash
**SecurityContext**: contains the authenticated token for the request; a configured repository may save it for later requests
**Two-phase token**: Filter creates unauthenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken with credentials only; provider creates authenticated version with authorities after verification

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In Spring Security's default form-login flow, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter handles the configured login-processing request and reads username and password form parameters. It creates an unauthenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken and sends it to AuthenticationManager. ProviderManager chooses a provider that supports the token. A common DaoAuthenticationProvider loads stored user details through UserDetailsService and checks the submitted password with PasswordEncoder.

On success, the provider returns an authenticated token with the principal and authorities. The filter puts it in the SecurityContext, calls the configured success handler, and saves the context through the configured SecurityContextRepository. In a normal session-based browser setup, an HTTP session repository makes that authentication available on later requests. On failure, the failure handler receives the AuthenticationException. The processing occurs in the security filter chain rather than a login controller, and persistence should be explained from the actual repository configuration rather than an old fixed filter name.

beats.content: When a user submits a login form, the POST request hits /login where UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter intercepts it first. The filter extracts the username and password and wraps them in an unauthenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.

That token is handed to AuthenticationManager, commonly ProviderManager, which chooses a supporting AuthenticationProvider. DaoAuthenticationProvider can load user details from the configured source and uses PasswordEncoder to verify the submitted password against the stored encoded value.

On success, the provider returns an authenticated token with the principal and authorities. The filter puts it in the SecurityContext, calls the success handler, and saves it through the configured SecurityContextRepository. A common browser configuration persists it in an HTTP session.

non-obvious: the filter creates an unauthenticated token; the provider creates the authenticated one. They're two different objects in two different states — that distinction matters when you're building JWT filters.

speakable_v2.cap: The filter reads the form, the manager selects a provider, the provider verifies the stored password, and the configured context repository decides whether authentication persists.

A bearer-token resource server has a different authentication flow and normally uses Spring Security's maintained bearer support.

question: What is the UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken in Spring Security?
title: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken — Before and After Authentication
direct_answer: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken is an Authentication implementation for username/password credentials. `unauthenticated(principal, credentials)` represents a request that still needs verification. After successful verification, an AuthenticationProvider normally returns an `authenticated(principal, credentials, authorities)` token. Spring can erase credentials afterward, and application code must not mark an unverified token as trusted.

sections.title: Understanding the Two-Phase Authentication Token
sections.content:
**UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken** implements **Authentication** for username/password credentials. Before verification, the filter creates an unauthenticated request token containing the submitted principal and credential. Current Spring Security exposes the `unauthenticated(...)` factory, and older code often uses the two-argument constructor. `isAuthenticated()` is false.

AuthenticationManager sends that request to a supporting provider. After verification, the provider normally returns a different authenticated token with the verified principal and granted authorities. Current code can use `authenticated(...)`; older examples use the three-argument constructor. Credentials may then be erased. The important boundary is trust: application code must not turn submitted data into an authenticated token without a real AuthenticationProvider or equivalent trusted verification. Standard OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens have their own authentication token types and Resource Server support.

sections.title: Two States, One Class
sections.content:
amber|Authentication request|~not verified|unauthenticated principal + credential|isAuthenticated false|sent to AuthenticationManager
emerald|Authentication result|~provider verified|authenticated principal + authorities|isAuthenticated true|credentials may be erased
blue|Trust boundary|~do not self-approve|provider chooses supported token|standard bearer auth uses its own token type|store only a verified result

sections.title: Creating and Using UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
When to Manually Create Authentication Tokens
sections.content:
Create an unauthenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken when custom username/password input must be submitted to AuthenticationManager. A supporting provider performs verification and returns the trusted result. In current code, prefer the named `unauthenticated(...)` and `authenticated(...)` factories because they state the intended trust level clearly.

Tests may create an authenticated token when deliberately arranging an already-authenticated SecurityContext. Production bearer, OAuth 2.0, or SSO integrations should normally use the Authentication implementation and maintained support designed for that protocol rather than forcing every identity into a username/password token.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trusting submitted data**: only a provider or other trusted authentication mechanism should produce the authenticated result.
- **Confusing factories or constructors**: the two-argument form is unauthenticated; the authorities form represents an already verified result.
- **Keeping credentials longer than needed**: ProviderManager can erase credentials after successful authentication; do not log or serialize raw passwords.
- **Calling setAuthenticated(true)**: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken rejects this shortcut. It can be changed back to false, so describing the entire object as immutable is also inaccurate.
- **Using it for every protocol**: bearer and OAuth 2.0 support use purpose-built Authentication types.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Named factories**: current code can use unauthenticated(...) for a request and authenticated(...) for a verified result
**Authentication flag**: application code cannot promote an unverified token with setAuthenticated(true); a token can be marked unauthenticated again
**Principal type**: submitted and verified principal objects depend on the provider and are not universally String then UserDetails
**Credential erasure**: ProviderManager can erase credentials after authentication to reduce exposure
**Filter creates unauthenticated**: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter creates unauthenticated token from form parameters and passes to AuthenticationManager

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken is an Authentication implementation for username/password credentials. The first state is an authentication request: `unauthenticated(principal, credentials)` has no granted authorities and returns false from isAuthenticated. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter creates this kind of request from form parameters and sends it to AuthenticationManager. A supporting provider verifies the credentials and normally returns a different authenticated token containing the verified principal and authorities. Current Spring Security provides an `authenticated(...)` factory, while older examples use the three-argument constructor. ProviderManager can erase credentials after success. The crucial rule is that application code must not create a trusted token from unverified input or call setAuthenticated(true) as a shortcut. Standard bearer JWT authentication should normally use Resource Server and its purpose-built Authentication type rather than a handwritten username/password token.
